name: Panty Ripper
description: Belize's unofficial national drink, with the least diplomatic name in the Caribbean: coconut rum and pineapple juice, over ice, on a beach.
funFact: Every bar from Caye Caulker to San Ignacio serves it, and every bartender tells a different story about the name — none of which they will repeat in front of your parents.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the coconut rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold pineapple juice.
Stir briefly to combine and garnish with a pineapple wedge.

name: Chiliguaro
description: A Costa Rican shot that behaves like a tiny Bloody Mary: guaro, tomato, lime and enough Salsa Lizano heat to wake the table up.
funFact: Salsa Lizano — a tangy Costa Rican condiment closer to brown sauce than hot sauce — is the ingredient that separates a real chiliguaro from a small Bloody Mary.

steps: Combine everything in a shaker with ice.
Shake briefly, about 8 seconds — you want it cold, not diluted.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

name: Guaro Sour
description: Costa Rica's national spirit taken the simplest possible way: guaro, lime, sugar, ice. Clean, sharp and dangerously easy in the heat.
funFact: Guaro — Cacique is the state-blessed brand — is a sugarcane spirit so central to Costa Rican life that its production was a government monopoly for most of the twentieth century.

steps: Rim a rocks glass with lime and salt.
Shake the guaro, lime juice and simple syrup hard with ice.
Strain into the rimmed glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
recipe.garnish: Lime wheel on a salted rim

name: Ponche de Frutas
description: Christmas in a mug across Guatemala: tropical fruit simmered with cinnamon and panela, spiked with rum at the last minute.
funFact: The fruit is meant to be eaten, not strained out — a Guatemalan ponche is served with a spoon, and the pieces at the bottom of the mug have been quietly soaking in rum all evening.

steps: Bring the water, panela and cinnamon sticks to a simmer in a large pot.
Add the diced fruit and raisins and simmer gently for about 40 minutes, until the fruit is soft and the liquid is amber.
Ladle the hot punch and a generous spoonful of fruit into each mug.
Add the rum to each mug individually, off the heat, so the alcohol survives.
Serve hot with a spoon.
recipe.garnish: A cinnamon stick and the stewed fruit

name: Guifiti
description: Garífuna herbal medicine that became a shot: raw rum steeped for weeks with roots, bark and spices until it turns dark, bitter and faintly medicinal.
funFact: Guifiti recipes are family property along the Honduran and Belizean Garífuna coast, traditionally prescribed for everything from stomach trouble to low spirits — the recipe is often only shared with an heir.

steps: Pack the roots, barks, cinnamon and cloves into a clean glass jar.
Cover completely with the overproof rum and seal.
Leave in a dark place for at least three weeks, shaking the jar every few days.
Strain out the solids, stir in the honey until dissolved, and rebottle.
Serve in small measures at room temperature.

name: Cazuela
description: A clay bowl the size of your head, packed with citrus, tequila and grapefruit soda, drunk through straws by everyone at the table. Sonora's answer to the punch bowl.
funFact: The bowl is the point: cazuelas are served in unglazed or glazed earthenware that keeps the drink cold, and in Hermosillo the bar brings it with the fruit still floating and scissors to cut more.

steps: Rim a large clay cazuela with lime and chilli salt.
Squeeze the orange, lime and grapefruit wedges into the bowl and drop the spent wedges in.
Fill with ice and pour over the tequila.
Top with grapefruit soda and stir once with a long spoon.
Serve in the middle of the table with straws for everyone.
recipe.garnish: The squeezed fruit wedges, left floating

name: Charro Negro
description: The Cuba Libre's tequila-drinking cousin: blanco, cola, lime, salt on the rim if you're doing it properly. Jalisco's default order when the Paloma feels like too much work.
funFact: Named for the charro — the Mexican horseman — and 'negro' for the cola; in Jalisco cantinas it is often built straight into the bottle-sized 'vitrolero' glass and shared.

steps: Run a lime wedge around the rim of a highball glass and roll it in salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the tequila and lime juice.
Top with cold cola and stir once, gently, to combine.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

name: Chelada
description: Beer, lime, salt, ice. That's it — no tomato, no sauces, no debate. The Michelada stripped back to the two things that actually matter on a hot afternoon.
funFact: Mexicans distinguish sharply between chelada (lime and salt only) and michelada (with tomato juice and sauces); ordering the wrong one in Monterrey will get you corrected, politely.

steps: Rim a chilled schooner or pint glass with lime and salt.
Fill the glass with ice cubes.
Add the lime juice.
Pour the cold lager down the side of the glass to keep the head under control.
Garnish with a lime wedge and top up from the bottle as you drink.
recipe.garnish: Lime wedge on a salted rim

name: La Bandera
description: Not one glass but three: lime, tequila, sangrita — green, white, red, the flag on the bar top. Sip across them in any order and argue about it afterwards.
funFact: The order is a national argument: most drinkers go lime, tequila, sangrita, but purists insist sangrita comes last only to cleanse, never to chase — the tequila is meant to be sipped, not shot.

steps: Pour the lime juice into the first caballito, the tequila into the second, and the sangrita into the third.
Line the three glasses up left to right so they read green, white, red.
Serve at cool room temperature — never over ice, and never mixed.
Sip the tequila slowly, alternating with small sips of lime and sangrita.
recipe.garnish: None — the three colours are the garnish

name: Mexican Firing Squad
description: A 1930s Mexico City sour that Charles H. Baker wrote down and the world then forgot for seventy years: tequila, lime, grenadine, a hard lash of Angostura.
funFact: Baker recorded it at La Cucaracha bar in 1937 in his 'Gentleman's Companion', calling it a drink of 'considerable authority' — one of the earliest tequila cocktails documented in English.

steps: Add the tequila, lime juice, grenadine and bitters to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Add a small splash of soda if you want it longer.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Mezcalita
description: The Margarita rebuilt on mezcal, which changes everything: the smoke arrives first, the lime cuts through it, and the agave finishes earthy rather than bright.
funFact: The rim is the tell: real Oaxacan service uses sal de gusano — salt ground with toasted agave worm and chilli — which tastes far better than its description suggests.

ingredients.item: Sal de gusano or chilli salt

steps: Rim a rocks glass with lime and sal de gusano, then set it aside.
Shake the mezcal, lime juice, agave syrup and orange liqueur hard with ice.
Strain into the rimmed glass over a large ice cube.
Garnish with a lime wheel and, if you have one, a dried chilli.

name: Submarino
description: A shot of tequila dropped, glass and all, into a beer. It sinks, it fizzes, it disappears — and then so does your evening.
glassware: Beer stein with a caballito inside
funFact: The same trick appears worldwide — Boilermaker in the US, U-Boot in Germany, Jägerbomb everywhere — but the Mexican version insists the submarine be tequila and the ocean be a light lager.

steps: Pour the beer into a large stein, leaving room at the top.
Fill a caballito shot glass with tequila.
Lower the shot glass carefully into the beer so it sinks upright.
Drink immediately, before the tequila fully diffuses.

name: Torito
description: Veracruz in a bottle: cane liquor whipped with condensed milk and fruit — peanut, guanabana, mango — until it drinks like a boozy milkshake with a suntan.
funFact: Toritos are sold from coolers along the Veracruz malecón in a dozen flavours; the peanut ('de cacahuate') version is the benchmark, and every vendor claims their abuela's ratio.

ingredients.item: Aguardiente de caña or white rum

steps: Add the milks and the peanut butter or fruit purée to a blender.
Pour in the cane spirit and add the ice.
Blend on high for about 30 seconds until completely smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled tumbler and serve immediately, before it separates.
Dust the top with ground cinnamon or crushed peanut.

name: Vampiro
description: Tequila, grapefruit soda and sangrita in one blood-red glass. Sweet, salty, citric and quietly spicy — the Paloma after it learned to bite.
funFact: The name means 'vampire' — for the colour, not the bite. It is the house drink of the bars around Tlaquepaque, where sangrita is made fresh daily and never contains tomato juice from a can.

steps: Rim a highball glass with lime and chilli salt, then fill it with ice.
Pour in the tequila, sangrita and lime juice.
Top with grapefruit soda.
Stir gently from the bottom once to marble the colours without fully mixing them.
Garnish with a lime wheel and an extra dusting of chilli salt.

name: Macuá
description: Nicaragua's official national cocktail, decided by public contest: white rum, guava, lemon and orange, tropical without tipping into syrup.
funFact: In 2006 Nicaragua's tourism board ran a nationwide competition to name a national drink; the winner was submitted by a paediatrician from Granada, and the Macuá is named after a local bird.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake for about 12 seconds until the outside of the tin frosts.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Seco con Leche
description: Panama's national spirit cut with milk over ice — sounds wrong, drinks like a cold, boozy horchata with a sugarcane backbone.
funFact: Seco Herrerano is triple-distilled from sugarcane and is Panama's national spirit; the milk serve — 'seco con leche' — is standard at interior festivals, especially during Carnaval.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Pour in the seco.
Top with cold whole milk.
Stir gently until the glass frosts, and serve straight away.
